youtube.title: The Famous Ford Pinto Memo Wasn't About the Pinto
youtube.description:
In 1977, Mother Jones published a Ford cost-benefit memo that valued a human life at $200,000 and compared an $11-per-vehicle fix ($137 million) with about $49.5 million for 180 burn deaths. It became the symbol of the Pinto scandal. But the memo covered all cars and light trucks, was about fuel leakage in rollover crashes rather than the Pinto's rear-end fires, and was prepared for federal regulators using the government's own value of a life. A federal review attributed 27 deaths to rear-end fuel fires in Pintos. The danger was real; the famous memo just wasn't the proof.

📂 Case File #057: The Pinto Memo

Sources: Gary T. Schwartz, "The Myth of the Ford Pinto Case," Rutgers Law Review (1991); Wikibooks, "Professionalism/The Ford Pinto Gas Tank Controversy" https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Professionalism/The_Ford_Pinto_Gas_Tank_Controversy ; Jalopnik, "Why the Ford Pinto didn't suck" https://jalopnik.com/5785674/why-the-ford-pinto-didnt-suck
